corn-frozen-cooked-fat-added-ns-as-to-fa.title: Corn, frozen, cooked, fat added, NS as to fat type

content.title: About
content.content: Corn is a globally cultivated grain. This product consists of frozen, cooked corn kernels with added vegetable fat to improve flavor and texture. It is ready to eat after heating and is often used as a side dish or ingredient in various recipes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn is one of the most widely consumed crops worldwide and forms a staple in many countries.
Frozen cooked kernels retain most of their vitamins and minerals thanks to rapid processing after harvest.
Adding fat enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins such as A and E.
Corn is used to produce starch, syrups, and bio‑fuel.
There are over 300 corn varieties differing in color, sweetness, and texture.

items.title: Rich source of carbohydrates
items.content: Corn provides a quick source of energy due to its high complex carbohydrate content.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestive health and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Corn supplies thiamin, niacin, and folate, which are important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Fat‑soluble vitamins
items.content: The added fat improves the bioavailability of vitamins A and E, beneficial for vision and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Corn provides magnesium, phosphorus, and potassium, supporting muscle and heart function.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn, ranging from skin rashes to severe symptoms.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Because the product contains added fat, people monitoring calorie intake should account for it in their diet.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Corn has a relatively high glycemic index, which can cause rapid blood sugar spikes in people with diabetes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The product is ready after heating in the microwave or on the stove. It can be added to salads, soups, stews, used as a side dish for meat or fish, or incorporated into tacos and burritos.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen corn at –18 °C or lower. Once thawed, use within 2–3 days and do not refreeze. Discard if it develops off‑odors or discoloration.

corned-beef-sandwich-on-white.title: Corned Beef Sandwich on White Bread

content.title: About
content.content: A corned beef sandwich on white bread is a classic quick snack. Thinly sliced, salt‑cured beef, brined with spices, is placed between two slices of soft white bread. The sandwich is usually served cold, sometimes with mustard or pickles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The term “corned beef” comes from the English word “corn,” referring to the large salt crystals used in the curing process.
Canned corned beef was first produced on a large scale in Ireland in the 19th century for export to the United States.
The sandwich became popular among sailors and travelers because it stays edible without refrigeration for long periods.
In the US, a classic variation often includes sauerkraut, Swiss cheese, and Russian dressing – the Reuben sandwich.
White bread used for this sandwich is typically crust‑less to provide a soft texture and easy bite.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Corned beef provides about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Beef is a good source of heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The sandwich offers a quick source of calories, useful during periods of high physical activity.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Corned beef can contain up to 2 g of salt per 100 g, which may raise blood pressure if consumed frequently.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: The product contains saturated fats, so individuals with cardiovascular concerns should limit portion size.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to beef or to additives in the brine.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Certain brands add nitrites and other preservatives, which can be undesirable in excess.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is typically eaten cold, cut in half. It can be enhanced with mustard, mayo, pickles, or lettuce. For a softer bite, lightly toast the bread.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the assembled sandwich refrigerated at 0–4 °C and consume within 2‑3 days. Store unopened canned corned beef in a cool, dry place; once opened, keep it in the fridge and use within 5‑7 days.

pasta-whole-grain-with-tomato-based-sauc.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Tomato Sauce, Poultry and Vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain pasta with tomato sauce, pieces of chicken meat and added vegetables is a ready‑to‑heat meal that warms up in a few minutes. The combination of whole‑grain pasta, tender chicken, tomato sauce and vegetables provides a balanced mix of protein, complex carbohydrates and vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole grain pasta contains more fiber and micronutrients than regular white pasta.
The tomato sauce is made from ripe tomatoes rich in lycopene, a powerful antioxidant.
Chicken meat is a source of easily digestible protein and vitamin B6.
Vegetables such as carrots, broccoli and bell pepper add vitamin C and extra dietary fiber.
The dish is designed for quick preparation: simply heat in a microwave or on the stove.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from whole grain pasta and vegetables helps maintain regular bowel movements.

items.title: Stabilizes blood sugar
items.content: Complex carbs release glucose slowly, preventing sharp spikes in blood sugar levels.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Chicken provides a complete set of amino acids needed for tissue repair.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes and vitamin C from vegetables help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: B‑vitamins, vitamin C and zinc contribute to normal immune system function.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: The product contains gluten; people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should choose a gluten‑free alternative.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The tomato sauce may contain added salt; those limiting sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: The dish includes a small amount of vegetable oil; consider the calories if following a low‑fat diet.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the meal in the microwave (2–3 minutes) or on the stovetop, stir, and serve hot. You can add fresh herbs, grated cheese, or a drizzle of olive oil to enhance flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store refrigerated at 0‑4 °C in the original packaging for up to 5 days after opening. The frozen version keeps for up to 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Pork ears are edible parts of a pig's head that are typically prepared by boiling, roasting, or smoking. They have a dense, gelatinous texture and a distinctive meaty flavor with a slight crispness when fried.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pork ears are used in traditional dishes around the world, such as Polish "ears in sour cream" and various Asian snacks.
In some cultures they are considered a delicacy because of their unique texture.
Ears are rich in collagen, which is why they are sometimes added to broths to improve gel strength.
They can be marinated, smoked, or dried, each method giving a different flavor profile.
In Russia pork ears are often served cold, thinly sliced as an appetizer.

items.title: Rich in collagen
items.content: Collagen in pork ears supports skin, joint, and connective‑tissue health.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: Pork ears provide a substantial amount of animal protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: They contain virtually no carbs, making them suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron from pork ears helps maintain normal hemoglobin levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Ears contain vitamin B12 and other B‑vitamins important for nervous system function.

items.title: Pig meat allergy
items.content: People allergic to pork may react to pork ears.

items.title: High sodium in cured versions
items.content: Ears that are heavily salted or cured can contribute to elevated blood pressure.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: Improper storage or insufficient cooking can lead to bacterial growth.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Pork ears contain a notable amount of fat, so they should be eaten in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pork ears can be boiled in broth, roasted in the oven, fried until crispy, or smoked. They are often sliced thin and served as a snack, added to salads, soups, or used as a garnish for main dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh ears refrigerated at 0‑4 °C for 2‑3 days. Frozen ears can be stored for up to 3 months. Before use, check that they have no off‑odor and no discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Tomatoes, canned, cooked are whole or diced tomatoes that have been heat‑treated and sealed in glass or metal jars with added salt, tomato paste, spices and sometimes sugar. The product is ready to eat and is commonly used in sauces, soups, stews and many other dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Canning preserves the flavor and most nutrients of tomatoes for months or years.
Canned tomatoes are usually blanched first, which makes skin removal easy.
In the United States, canned tomatoes are one of the “five basic vegetables” frequently served in school meals.
Tomatoes can be “pelleted” – ground into a puree that simplifies later cooking.
Thermal processing increases the bioavailability of lycopene compared with fresh tomatoes.

items.title: Rich in lycopene
items.content: Lycopene is a powerful antioxidant that supports heart health and may lower the risk of certain cancers.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber in tomatoes promotes healthy bowel function and satiety.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Canned tomatoes are a low‑calorie food, suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports muscle function.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some canned tomato varieties contain added salt, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Bisphenol A (BPA)
items.content: Cans lined with BPA can leach chemicals; choose BPA‑free or glass containers when possible.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes.

items.title: Added sugar
items.content: Certain recipes add sugar to balance acidity; this should be considered for sugar‑controlled diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned tomatoes can be added to pasta sauces, soups, chili, stews, pizza, and salads. They also serve as a base for tomato juice or paste. The product is ready to eat, but you may heat it if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened jars in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the contents in a sealed container in the refrigerator and use within 5‑7 days. Discard if the jar is bulging, leaking, or the tomatoes develop an off‑odor.
